title: Processes vs Threads, Context Switching & Deadlocks
content: A process is an executing program instance with its own isolated virtual memory address space (text, data, heap, stack). A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares the heap, global variables, and open file descriptors with sibling threads while maintaining its own program counter and stack. Coffman conditions for deadlocks: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption, 4. Circular Wait. Resolving deadlocks: Banker's algorithm, lock ordering, or timeout preemption.
key_takeaways: Processes have isolated address spaces; threads share heap and state
Context switches between processes incur TLB flush penalties
Four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlocks

title: TCP vs UDP, Three-Way Handshake & OSI Model
content: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable protocol that guarantees ordered delivery through sequence numbers, flow control (sliding window), and congestion control (Slow Start, AIMD). The TCP connection initiates via a three-way handshake: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK, and closes via FIN -> ACK -> FIN -> ACK. UDP is connectionless and lightweight with zero transmission guarantees, suitable for real-time streaming, DNS, and VoIP where low latency outweighs packet loss.
key_takeaways: TCP three-way handshake establishes bidirectional sequence numbers
Sliding window regulates receiver buffer capacity
UDP offers minimal overhead without retransmission delay
